Since early 2018 I have held various roles in crypto, working mostly in research and formal verification. My original interests in crypto were in consensus algorithms and formal verification frameworks for verifying smart contracts. When I started, those frameworks and tools were in their infancy, K Framework being the only tool at the time to my knowledge that was production-ready for actual smart contracts.
Over time, I became interested in the financial applications of smart contracts and I did my PhD in verification strategies for financial smart contracts.
Along the way, I became deeply interested in type theory and proof assistants, and these days am interested broadly in theorem-proving, whether applied to software or formalized maths.
In my day-to-day, I still do a lot of work in the design, construction, and formal verification of smart contracts.

I started working in crypto during the two years between my MSc and my PhD. My first job was at a small, Utah-based crypto startup called Pyrofex, which was mostly providing consulting services to the RChain co-op at the time. I was tasked with building the formal semantics for rholang, the smart contracting language on RChain, in K Framework in order to formally verify rholang contracts down the line.

RChain, famously, encountered sudden and urgent financial problems because of a questionable set of decisions from the co-op's president, Greg Meredith, which necessitated a split between RChain and Pyrofex. We then pivoted to consensus-level research, designed our own layer-one blockchain and consensus protocol.

Sadly, we ran out of money, and I had to look for a new job for the few months before my PhD started. I took a short internship with Digital Asset, working in Zurich and New York, and implementing an experimental currency on their blockchain-esque project Canton.

During my PhD, I took several part-time jobs with various crypto startups. My work ranged from research and formal verification, to DeFi protocol modeling and design, to zero-knowledge proofs, to business development. Each of my jobs during the PhD informed my research and helped to broaden and sharpen my thinking. I took the last year of my PhD to focus fully on writing up and submitting.

Since my PhD has ended, I went through a process of unifying my various interests in people, proofs, smart contracts, digital money, and zero-knowledge proofs. I took a job with Certora straight out of my PhD, doing a mix of formally verifying smart contracts and project managmenet/business development/product development/client support. Ultimately, it became clear that Certora was not the place that I was going to do my best work, so early 2025 we parted ways.

I then took some temporary contract work over the summer of 2025 building, designing, and verifying DeFi protocols (my specific area of expertise) while I looked for something that I can truly sink my teeth into and that would define the next period of my career.
As of November 2025 I joined the Ethereum Foundation, working on Protocol Snarkification. This mostly consists of formally specifying and verifying ZK primitives in Lean.

A systematic study of the cryptography and machine architecture that zkVMs and SNARKs are built from, topic by topic. It is the theory behind the snarkification work: ArkLib, CompPoly, and Clean formalise these protocols in Lean, and formalisation rewards local knowledge — a folding lemma can be proved without holding the whole argument in view. The purpose of a corpus like this one is to hold the whole argument.

The spine is the pipeline every modern proof system follows. A computation becomes a constraint system; the constraint system becomes an interactive oracle proof; the oracles are realised by commitments; the interaction is removed by Fiat–Shamir; the result is made recursive and wrapped around a virtual machine. Each section below is one stage of that pipeline, which is also roughly how ArkLib is organised — so a page here usually has a Lean file behind it.

Every leaf has the same shape: what the page covers, the questions it should answer, and where to read. A page is complete when its subject can be reconstructed from it without the sources — for a protocol, that means the theorem stated with its assumptions, and what breaks when one of them is dropped.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The vocabulary layer. FRI, Spartan, and WHIR are instances of the same handful of definitions, and much of what is confusing in a paper is a confusion about which definition is in play: which soundness notion, in which oracle model, against which adversary.

Two questions this section exists to answer. What does a security proof for a SNARK actually establish? And at which step of the compilation from interactive protocol to deployed system does the security get lost?

The chain of definitions that everything else is stated in terms of, ending at the interactive oracle reduction that ArkLib takes as primitive. Proof does different work here than it does in proposition and proof: a SNARK convinces a verifier with high probability under stated assumptions, and is not a derivation.

Questions this page should answer:
Interactive proof, argument (prover computationally bounded), PCP, IOP, oracle reduction — what each relaxation buys.
Completeness: honest prover, true statement, accept. Perfect versus statistical, and why it is not the bound that matters.
Where succinct and of knowledge enter, and what each costs the construction.
Public-coin versus private-coin, and why every deployed system is public-coin.
The knowledge extractor: what it is handed, what it must produce, and why rewinding is a problem in the non-interactive setting.
Zero-knowledge — honest-verifier versus malicious, as the sigma protocols exhibit the distinction, and how much of it a zkVM actually needs. Mostly these systems are bought for succinctness.
Reading: ArkLib/OracleReduction/Basic.lean as the definitional reference; Thaler, Proofs, Arguments, and Zero-Knowledge, for the textbook chain.

A sigma protocol is a three-move public-coin proof of knowledge. It is the smallest object carrying all three of the properties a security theorem for a proof system has to state, which is why the definitions in this section are easiest to read against one, and why Schnorr is worth holding in mind throughout.

The relation. Fix a relation R \subseteq X \times W. The public statement is x \in X; the witness is w with (x, w) \in R. The prover holds both, the verifier only x. What is proved is not that x has a witness but that the prover knows one, which is why knowledge soundness rather than soundness is the property with content here.

The three messages.
The prover sends a commitment a.
The verifier sends a challenge e, drawn uniformly from a challenge set E of size N and independent of a. That independence is what public-coin means: the verifier's message is its randomness, sent in the clear.
The prover sends a response z. The verifier accepts exactly when an acceptance predicate V(x, a, e, z) holds. It keeps no state beyond the transcript, so (a, e, z) is accepting or not on its own terms, independently of how it was produced. That is what makes a transcript simulable, and what makes two of them subtractable.
Completeness. An honest prover holding w with (x, w) \in R is accepted. In this family it holds with probability one; completeness is where the general definition and its failure modes live.

Special soundness. From two accepting transcripts (a, e, z) and (a, e', z') sharing the commitment, with e \neq e', an efficient algorithm computes a w with (x, w) \in R. This is a condition on the algebra of V, not a probability bound, so checking it means exhibiting the computation rather than arguing about adversaries. Knowledge soundness with error 1/N follows generically, by rewinding: run the prover, fork it at the challenge, and collect a second accepting transcript on the same a. Special soundness has the multi-round generalisation and what the rewinding costs once the protocol is made non-interactive.

Special honest-verifier zero knowledge. An efficient simulator, given x and a challenge e fixed in advance, outputs an accepting transcript (a, e, z) distributed exactly as a real one, with no witness. Both qualifiers do work. Special means the simulator is handed e rather than choosing it, which is what lets the property survive Fiat–Shamir. Honest-verifier means the guarantee covers a verifier that draws e uniformly; a malicious verifier choosing e as a function of a is outside the definition, and closing that gap takes more than the three moves provide.
The definition. A three-move public-coin protocol satisfying completeness, special soundness, and special honest-verifier zero knowledge is a sigma protocol for R.

Three things beyond the definition are worth knowing. Sigma protocols compose: Cramer, Damgård, and Schoenmakers showed that conjunctions and disjunctions of relations have sigma protocols assembled from those for the parts, which is where ring signatures and the older range proofs come from. Fiat–Shamir applied to one gives a signature scheme, Schnorr signatures being the transform of the Schnorr protocol. And the multi-round protocols the rest of this corpus is about are the generalisation — (k_1, \dots , k_\mu )-special soundness replaces the pair of transcripts with a tree, at which point a sigma protocol is the case \mu = 1, k_1 = 2.

Schnorr is the worked example of a sigma protocol: three messages in which a prover convinces a verifier that it knows the discrete logarithm of a group element, and reveals nothing else. Zero-knowledge proof of knowledge is nearly the right name for it, but under-specifies it twice. Of knowledge is the load-bearing half — every element of a cyclic group generated by g has a discrete logarithm, so the statement has no false instances and plain soundness says nothing about it. And the zero-knowledge is special honest-verifier: the simulator below needs the challenge in advance and assumes it was drawn uniformly. Honest-verifier zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of a discrete logarithm is the accurate mouthful.

The setting is a cyclic group G of prime order q with generator g, in which the discrete logarithm is hard. The statement is a group element h \in G; the witness is the exponent w \in \mathbb {Z}_q with g^w = h.

The protocol:
The prover draws r uniformly from \mathbb {Z}_q and sends the commitment a = g^r.
The verifier draws a challenge e uniformly from \mathbb {Z}_q and sends it.
The prover sends the response z = r + e w \bmod q. The verifier accepts exactly when
Completeness is the exponent arithmetic. Substituting z = r + ew,
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: g^z = g^{r + e w} = g^r (g^w)^e = a \cdot h^e,
fr:mainmatter.html:p: so an honest prover is always accepted and the completeness error is zero.
Special soundness is one subtraction. Two accepting transcripts (a, e, z) and (a, e', z') on the same commitment satisfy g^z = a h^e and g^{z'} = a h^{e'}. Dividing the first by the second cancels a:
Since q is prime and e \neq e', the difference e - e' is invertible in \mathbb {Z}_q, so

is the discrete logarithm of h. That is the extractor in full: subtract, invert, stop. Two field operations, and no assumption about the prover beyond its having produced the two transcripts. It is also where the prime order earns its keep — at composite order e - e' may fail to be invertible and the step collapses.

Special honest-verifier zero knowledge is the same equation read backwards. Given h and a challenge e, the simulator draws z uniformly from \mathbb {Z}_q and sets a = g^z h^{-e}, so the transcript (a, e, z) satisfies the verification equation by construction. The distribution matches exactly, not approximately. In a real transcript r is uniform, hence z = r + ew is uniform and independent of e, and a is then pinned down by z and e through the verification equation. Both distributions are therefore uniform z with a determined, so they are the same distribution — and w cannot be recovered from a simulated transcript because it never entered.

Three consequences outside the definition. Fiat–Shamir replaces the verifier with a hash, e = H(g, h, a), turning the protocol into the Schnorr signature scheme — deployed as Ed25519 and, since Taproot, as BIP-340 in Bitcoin — and the (Q+1)\kappa bound of special soundness is what makes the transformed protocol analysable at all. Nonce reuse is the extractor turned against its owner: two signatures sharing a under different challenges hand over w by the subtraction above, which is how signing keys have actually been lost. And the knowledge error 1/q is a claim about the challenge set, not the group — a prover with no witness can guess a challenge, simulate a transcript for it, and win with that probability, so a small challenge space has to be repeated rather than trusted.

Sources: Schnorr, Efficient Signature Generation by Smart Cards (Journal of Cryptology, 1991); Damgård, On Σ-protocols, for the extraction and simulation written out; VCV-io formalises sigma protocols and the Fiat–Shamir transform in Lean.

Sources: Damgård, On Σ-protocols, for the definitions in this shape; Cramer, Damgård, and Schoenmakers, Proofs of Partial Knowledge and Simplified Design of Witness Hiding Protocols (CRYPTO 1994), for the composition; Thaler, Proofs, Arguments, and Zero-Knowledge.

An honest prover with a true statement is accepted, except with small probability — usually with probability one. Unlike soundness this is one property, not a family, and compilation preserves it. The obligation that fails is one layer down: a circuit is complete when every honest execution has a satisfying witness, which is what Clean treats as separate from soundness.

Questions this page should answer:
The definition, and the completeness error. When a protocol is perfectly complete and when it is not.
How completeness composes under oracle reductions.
What Fiat–Shamir and BCS do to it.
Circuit completeness versus protocol completeness, and the form of the obligation in Clean.
Where ArkLib states it.
Sources: Thaler, Proofs, Arguments, and Zero-Knowledge; ArkLib (OracleReduction).

Soundness is the claim that a cheating prover cannot make the verifier accept a false statement, except with small probability. Completeness is the matching guarantee for an honest prover with a true statement, and is almost never where a protocol fails. The definition has to name the adversary: which provers, in which game, with which oracles.

Sound names a family of properties. Most papers prove the weakest member; compilation (interactive protocol to deployed non-interactive argument) needs a stronger one. Khovratovich, Rothblum, and Soukhanov proved false statements against a deployed GKR-based argument whose interactive soundness was never in question. The interactive theorem was true; it was the wrong theorem.

The notions, weakest first, for a public-coin protocol \Pi with \mu challenge rounds deciding membership in a language L.
Soundness — no prover convinces the verifier of a false statement except with probability at most \epsilon . Which provers are admitted is the whole content of the definition: unbounded ones make \Pi a proof, computationally bounded ones an argument.
Knowledge soundness — an efficient extractor recovers a witness from any prover that convinces V. Strictly stronger, and the only one of the two with content when every statement is in the language.
Special soundness — a combinatorial condition on the verifier: a tree of accepting transcripts, branching at each challenge round, yields a witness. Not a security guarantee but a hypothesis that implies one, and checkable by inspecting the algebra. Lattice protocols, whose challenges are vectors, run on a coordinate-wise variant that branches per coordinate rather than per challenge.
Round-by-round soundness — every transcript prefix carries a state, a false statement starts doomed, and a single round escapes doom with probability at most \epsilon _i.
State-restoration soundness — soundness against a prover that may return to any prefix it has already built and draw a fresh challenge there, as often as its budget allows. Three qualifiers cut across all five and are quoted less often than they should be: whether the statement is fixed before the hash function or chosen after, whether the extractor may rewind or must work straightline, and which oracles the adversary is given. A soundness claim missing any of the three is not yet a claim.

The implications make the family a hierarchy rather than a list. Knowledge soundness implies soundness once the knowledge error is below one. Round-by-round soundness implies soundness with error \sum _{i=1}^{\mu } \epsilon _i, by a union bound over rounds. State-restoration soundness implies soundness with the error preserved, and is equivalent to round-by-round soundness up to a polynomial loss. Special soundness implies round-by-round soundness — Block, Garreta, Tiwari, and Zając prove this for generalised forms of both. Each notion has a knowledge counterpart, and round-by-round knowledge soundness implies both round-by-round soundness and plain knowledge soundness. ArkLib states these arrows as theorems in OracleReduction/Security/Implications.lean — knowledge soundness to soundness, round-by-round to plain in both directions, state restoration to both — which is a useful check on the decomposition, since each arrow has to be proved rather than asserted.

Compilation is where a notion gets chosen, not merely inherited. Sequential composition preserves plain soundness, with the errors accumulating. The Fiat–Shamir transform does not: analysed from plain soundness alone, a (2\mu +1)-move protocol loses a factor Q^\mu in the adversary's random-oracle query count Q, which says nothing at all for the twenty-odd rounds of a folding argument. From special soundness the loss is Q+1 regardless of round count; from round-by-round soundness it is likewise linear in Q. The BCS transform is analysed against state restoration directly. A many-round protocol therefore has to be analysed round-by-round from the start, because an end-to-end soundness bound cannot be repaired after the fact.

Soundness quantifies over a class of provers, and the choice of class is the whole content of the definition. A verifier V for a language L is sound with error \epsilon if for every x \notin L and every admitted prover strategy P^*, \Pr (\langle P^*, V\rangle (x) = 1) \le \epsilon . Admitting all strategies gives an interactive proof; admitting only polynomial-time ones gives an argument. Every deployed system is an argument, because statistical soundness with communication shorter than the witness would carry complexity-theoretic consequences nobody expects, and succinctness is the property these systems are bought for.

Soundness is vacuous whenever the language is trivial. "There is an a with g^a = h" holds for every h in a cyclic group, so a Schnorr proof has no false statements to be sound about, and the property the application wants — that this prover holds a — is not soundness at all. Knowledge soundness is the property with content: there is an efficient extractor E such that any P^* convincing V with probability \epsilon ^* yields a witness from E with probability at least \epsilon ^* - \kappa , where \kappa is the knowledge error. It implies soundness whenever \kappa < 1, since for x \notin L there is no witness to extract and acceptance is bounded by \kappa — ArkLib's knowledgeSoundness_implies_soundness.

It is also what makes recursion possible. The outer circuit's statement is that a valid inner proof exists, which is a claim about the existence of a string rather than about the computation anyone cares about; only an extractor turns it back into the inner claim. Soundness of the outer proof would establish nothing about the inner one, which is why every folding and aggregation scheme is stated with a knowledge hypothesis and why the extractors compose one layer at a time.

What the extractor is handed is the distinction that survives compilation. A rewinding extractor runs P^* repeatedly from a saved state with fresh challenges; this is how special soundness yields extraction, and it is unobjectionable while the protocol is interactive. A straightline extractor is given one transcript, plus the prover's and verifier's oracle query logs, and must produce the witness without re-running anything. After Fiat–Shamir the prover is a single algorithm querying a hash, so the query log is available and rewinding is not free: rewinding a non-interactive prover is exactly what the Q^\mu loss in the naive analysis pays for.

ArkLib takes straightline extraction as primary. Extractor.Straightline is deterministic, with type \mathrm {StmtIn} \to \mathrm {WitOut} \to \mathrm {FullTranscript} \to \mathrm {QueryLog} \to \mathrm {QueryLog} \to \mathrm {WitIn} in the option monad over the oracle computation, and knowledgeSoundness is stated as the existence of such an extractor. Rewinding lives in a separate file and is still unfinished, for a reason worth recording: the extractor needs to update and maintain the prover's state across its queries, which the current representation of a prover does not support. That the harder definition is the one that resisted formalisation is not a coincidence — rewinding is where informal proofs are most often loose about what the extractor may do.

Two refinements belong to the same layer. Witness-extended emulation — Lindell's formulation, and the one the Bulletproofs lineage proves — asks the extractor to reproduce the transcript distribution as well as the witness, which is what composition needs. And soundness may be stated with the statement fixed in advance or chosen adaptively after the hash function is public; the two differ by more than a constant, and the difference is where the practical Fiat–Shamir attacks live.
Reading: ArkLib/OracleReduction/Security/Basic.lean and Rewinding.lean; Thaler, Proofs, Arguments, and Zero-Knowledge, for the textbook development.

Special soundness is a property of the verifier's acceptance predicate, not a probability bound, which is why it is the workhorse. For a three-move sigma protocol it says: from two accepting transcripts (a, c, z) and (a, c', z') sharing the first message with c \neq c', a witness can be computed in polynomial time. Checking it means exhibiting that computation — for Schnorr, subtracting two linear equations — so it is verifiable by inspecting the algebra rather than by a probabilistic argument. Knowledge soundness then follows generically, with a rewinding extractor that collects the transcripts it needs.

The multi-round generalisation is (k_1, \dots , k_\mu )-special soundness. Instead of a pair of transcripts the extractor is given a tree: at the i-th challenge round each node branches k_i ways with pairwise distinct challenges, and the tree of accepting leaves yields a witness. Attema and Fehr computed the resulting knowledge error exactly for challenge sets of sizes N_1, \dots , N_\mu ; it is at most \sum _{i=1}^{\mu } (k_i - 1)/N_i, which is the bound worth remembering. Two special soundness at each of \mu rounds over a field of size q costs \mu / q, and the tree has \prod _i k_i leaves, so the extractor's cost is what limits how large the k_i can be.

The reason to care is the Fiat–Shamir accounting. Attema, Fehr, and Klooß showed that the Fiat–Shamir transform of a (k_1, \dots , k_\mu )-special-sound protocol has knowledge error (Q+1)\kappa against an adversary making Q random-oracle queries, where \kappa is the interactive knowledge error — linear in Q and independent of the number of rounds. The general bound for a (2\mu +1)-move protocol is Q^\mu . For any protocol with more than a handful of rounds that is the difference between a security claim and none, and it is bought entirely by strengthening the hypothesis from soundness to special soundness.

The lattice protocols needed the tree reshaped rather than widened. Their challenges are vectors of \ell _i coordinates, and extraction works coordinate by coordinate: two accepting transcripts that differ in one coordinate alone subtract to an equation in the matching block of the witness. Transcripts that differ everywhere subtract to nothing usable. Coordinate-wise special soundness, introduced by Fenzi, Moghaddas, and Nguyen for their lattice polynomial commitment, makes this the branching condition: each node at round i has \ell _i(k_i - 1) + 1 children — a central challenge vector, plus k_i - 1 others per coordinate differing from it in that coordinate only. The knowledge error is at most \sum _{i=1}^{\mu } \ell _i k_i / N_i^{\ell _i} for coordinates drawn from sets of size N_i, the tree stays polynomially small, and taking every \ell _i = 1 recovers plain special soundness. Their Fiat–Shamir theorem carries over too, so the linear-in-Q accounting above survives the generalisation. Hachi, a lattice multilinear commitment refining Greyhound, states its whole security analysis in this form — down to bundling a pair of sumcheck challenge points into one vector of logarithmically many coordinates, so that a coordinate-wise tree supplies enough distinct roots to force a constraint polynomial to vanish.

ArkLib formalises both through transcript trees generic in a shape. distinctShape k is the shape with branching arity k_i whose node predicate requires the k_i sibling challenges at each round to be pairwise distinct, and Verifier.specialSound is the instance of the shape-generic treeSpecialSound at that shape; CoordinateWiseSpecialSoundness is the coordinate-wise condition above, and ArkLib proves that plain special soundness is the distinctShape case of it. The genericity is not gratuitous: real protocols keep needing branching conditions other than "all siblings differ."

Where special soundness stops is the FRI family. Extraction there does not go through a transcript tree at all — it goes through list decoding, recovering a codeword close to the prover's oracles, and the argument's structure is a distance bound rather than a system of equations. That is why the low-degree testing pages are analysed round-by-round instead, and why the two techniques appear side by side in the same system: the algebraic components get special soundness, the proximity components get a state function.

Sources: Fiat–Shamir Transformation of Multi-Round Interactive Proofs (Attema, Fehr, Klooß) for the (Q+1)\kappa bound, Lattice-Based Polynomial Commitments: Towards Asymptotic and Concrete Efficiency (Fenzi, Moghaddas, Nguyen) for coordinate-wise special soundness and its interactive and Fiat–Shamir knowledge theorems, Hachi (Nguyen, O'Rourke, Zhang) for the notion in working use, On Soundness Notions for Interactive Oracle Proofs for the generalised versions and their implications, and ArkLib/OracleReduction/Security/SpecialSoundness.lean.

Round-by-round soundness replaces one global bound with a bound per round, and that locality is what makes it compile. Canetti, Chen, Holmgren, Lombardi, Rothblum, and Rothblum introduced it to prove Fiat–Shamir secure under an assumption on the hash function rather than by fiat. The definition asks for a state function: a labelling of each pair (statement, transcript prefix) as doomed or not, satisfying three conditions.
If x \notin L, the empty transcript is doomed.
If a prefix is doomed, it stays doomed after the prover's next message — unconditionally, for every message — and after the following challenge except with probability at most \epsilon _i over that challenge.
A doomed complete transcript is rejected. Plain soundness follows with error \sum _{i=1}^{\mu } \epsilon _i: to be accepted from a false statement the transcript must escape doom at some round, and the sum is a union bound over the rounds where that can happen.

Splitting the two propagation conditions is the point of the definition. A prover message can never help — only the verifier's randomness can undoom a prefix — so the entire error budget sits on the challenge rounds, one \epsilon _i apiece. An adversary who grinds on a hash is choosing among candidate challenges at some round, and the round-by-round bound says what each attempt is worth. A monolithic soundness bound cannot: it constrains the honest interaction and says nothing about a prover that retries one round.

In the standard model the payoff is a theorem. Canetti et al. proved that \mathrm {FS}(\Pi , \mathcal {H}) is computationally sound whenever \Pi is round-by-round sound and \mathcal {H} is correlation intractable for the relation derived from the state function. In the random oracle model the compilation loss is linear in the adversary's query count. Either way the hypothesis is round-by-round soundness, which is why the notion appears in every modern security proof of a deployed hash-based system and why a paper proving only end-to-end soundness has not yet said anything about its own non-interactive version.

Round-by-round knowledge soundness adds a round-by-round extractor to the state function, so that a doomed prefix witnesses the impossibility of extraction rather than the falsity of a statement. This is the form the practical results take. Block, Garreta, Katz, Thaler, Tiwari, and Zając proved round-by-round soundness and round-by-round knowledge soundness for FRI and batched FRI, and for a class they call \delta -correlated protocols — which covers Plonky2, Redshift, ethSTARK, and RISC Zero — giving the first formal Fiat–Shamir security proof for FRI. Their reduction is the reusable part: a \delta -correlated protocol that is round-by-round sound under the assumption that adversaries send low-degree polynomials is round-by-round sound in general.

The cost of the notion is that a proof has to exhibit the state function, and for the interesting protocols that is the whole difficulty. For FRI it is a statement about the distance from the prover's oracle to the Reed–Solomon code, so the decoding regime and the proximity gap available in that regime appear inside \epsilon _i. This is the seam where a conjecture enters a deployed security claim, and it enters through the round-by-round error rather than anywhere more visible.

ArkLib's OracleReduction/Security/RoundByRound.lean makes the state function a structure — toFun of type (m : \mathrm {Fin}(n+1)) \to \mathrm {StmtIn} \to \mathrm {Transcript}\, m \to \mathrm {Prop}, with fields toFun_empty, toFun_next, and toFun_full for the three conditions — and defines rbrSoundness as a bound on the probability of a bad transition at each challenge index. rbrKnowledgeSoundness additionally carries intermediate witness types, a round-by-round extractor, and a knowledge state function. Because ArkLib works with reductions rather than proofs, both are stated relative to an input and an output language.

Sources: Canetti, Chen, Holmgren, Lombardi, Rothblum, and Rothblum, Fiat–Shamir: from practice to theory (STOC 2019); Fiat–Shamir Security of FRI and Related SNARKs; ArkLib/OracleReduction/Security/RoundByRound.lean.

State-restoration soundness models the one power Fiat–Shamir hands the prover: the ability to retry. In the state-restoration game the prover builds transcripts against a challenge oracle that, given a statement and any prefix, returns that prefix's challenge; it may return to any prefix it has already constructed, send a different message, and receive the corresponding challenge, as many times as its budget allows. It wins if any completed transcript is accepting for a false statement. Ben-Sasson, Chiesa, and Spooner introduced the notion with the BCS transform, and it is the hypothesis that transform is proved against.

The correspondence with the compiled protocol is exact rather than analogical. A non-interactive prover holding the hash computes the challenge for any prefix it likes by querying the oracle, so the ordering of an interactive execution is not enforced — nothing stops it from abandoning a prefix and trying another message at the same point. State-restoration soundness assumes precisely that adversary and no more, which is why the notion is more convenient than plain soundness at the compilation step and less convenient anywhere else.

Holmgren proved that round-by-round soundness and soundness against state-restoration attacks are equivalent, up to a polynomial loss in the number of restoration attempts. The two notions are therefore interchangeable as hypotheses, and the choice between them is a choice of proof convenience: round-by-round is local, so it is what a paper proves; state restoration names the adversary, so it is what a bound on real attack cost is stated against. Knowing they coincide is what licenses moving between the two halves of a security argument.

The budget is where engineering enters. The adversary's success probability scales with the number of restoration attempts, so anything that makes an attempt expensive buys bits. Proof-of-work grinding is exactly this: requiring each prover message to be accompanied by a nonce whose hash has b leading zeros means an adversary with t hash evaluations gets about t/2^b attempts rather than t, and the b bits show up in the state-restoration bound and nowhere else in the protocol. It is also why a deployed security level cannot be read off the interactive analysis alone.

Salting works in the same accounting. ArkLib's Salt.lean adds per-message randomness to a protocol, and srSoundness_addSalt_implies_srSoundness_original runs in the direction that makes salting free to assume: state-restoration soundness of the salted protocol gives it for the original, with the knowledge version proved alongside. Both state-restoration notions then imply their straightline counterparts with the error preserved — srSoundness_implies_soundness and srKnowledgeSoundness_implies_knowledgeSoundness — so the state-restoration analysis is the strongest of the hash-based statements and everything else in the chain follows from it.
Sources: Ben-Sasson, Chiesa, and Spooner, Interactive Oracle Proofs (TCC 2016); On Round-By-Round Soundness and State Restoration Attacks; ArkLib/OracleReduction/Security/StateRestoration.lean.

fr:title.text: From Soundness Error to Bits of Security

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: From Soundness Error to Bits of Security

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A bit-security figure is a claim about a bound, and two conventions for turning an error into bits are both in circulation. The bound for a hash-based argument has the shape

with t the adversary's hash evaluations and \epsilon _{\mathrm {sr}} the state-restoration error of one attempt. One convention reads "\lambda bits" as \epsilon _{\mathrm {sr}} \le 2^{-\lambda }; the other reads it as the requirement that success probability stay below t/2^{\lambda } for every t, so that 2^{\lambda } work is needed for constant success. The two differ by exactly the factor t, and t is not small: at a query budget of 2^{60}, a system quoting 100 bits under the first convention offers 2^{-40} against that adversary. Neither convention is wrong, and a number quoted without saying which is not yet information.

The terms in the bound have different provenances, which is the part worth holding in view when reading a parameter table.
Rounds add: the round-by-round errors sum to \epsilon _{\mathrm {sr}} = \sum _i \epsilon _i, so a protocol with many cheap rounds pays for each of them.
Repetitions multiply: r independent repetitions take an error \epsilon to \epsilon ^r. For the repeated queries inside a low-rate FRI configuration this is where most of the security level comes from.
Compilation multiplies by the query budget, as above — this is the t that separates the two conventions.
Grinding divides: b bits of proof-of-work reduce an adversary's t hash evaluations to about t/2^{b} state-restoration attempts.
The commitment contributes its own term, a Merkle collision probability of order t^2/2^{n} for an n-bit digest. This is the reason a 128-bit target is paired with a 256-bit hash rather than a 128-bit one. The claimed level is set by the largest term, so an analysis that is tight on four of them and loose on the fifth has established only what the loose one gives.

Recursion is where this becomes hard to audit. Errors add across layers, and the outermost wrapping proof — usually a different proof system over a different field, chosen for on-chain verification cost rather than for its security margin — often contributes the dominant term. A system whose inner argument is analysed to 128 bits and whose wrapper is not analysed at all has an unknown security level, not a 128-bit one.

Then there is the question of which \epsilon _i to use, and it does not have a single answer: the same protocol admits different round-by-round errors depending on how far past the unique-decoding radius the analysis is willing to reason, and the parameters shipped in production sit where the argument is conjectural. That is the subject of soundness regimes and proximity gaps, and the practical consequence is that a deployed figure should be quoted twice, provably and conjecturally. The ethSTARK documentation does this, and is the deployment document I would point to as the model.

None of this measures the best known attack. Every number here bounds what a proof can rule out, and the gap between that bound and the cheapest actual forgery is not quantified anywhere in this literature — which is a reasonable position for a security argument to take, and a bad one to forget when comparing a proof system's "128 bits" against a hash function's. What the production parameters actually add up to is a separate page.

Whether the statement is fixed before the hash function is public or chosen after it is the qualifier the Fiat–Shamir attacks turn on, and it is usually left implicit. This page should make the distinction explicit and say which side deployed claims are on.

Questions this page should answer:
Non-adaptive and adaptive soundness stated side by side, for both the plain and the knowledge versions.
Why the Khovratovich–Rothblum–Soukhanov attack is an adaptive-soundness attack: it embeds the hash function into the circuit, which is a statement chosen after the hash is known.
What adaptivity costs in the random oracle model, and whether the loss is a constant, a factor of the query count, or worse.
Block, Garreta, Tiwari, and Zając: a special-sound IOP Fiat–Shamir-compiles to an adaptively sound non-interactive proof in the QROM. What that covers and what it does not.
Whether a zkVM's statement is genuinely fixed at circuit-compile time in deployment — including precompiles and any circuit chosen by an untrusted party — and who is responsible for checking.
Sources: How to Prove False Statements, On Soundness Notions for Interactive Oracle Proofs.

Repetition is how most of a security level is actually bought, and the theorem licensing it is narrower than the practice suggests. The rate at which error decays depends on the round count and on whether the protocol is public-coin, and there are counterexamples where it does not decay at all.

Questions this page should answer:
Sequential and parallel repetition, and when r repetitions take a soundness error \epsilon to \epsilon ^r.
Bellare, Impagliazzo, and Naor's four-message argument whose n-fold parallel repetition keeps error 1/2, and Pietrzak and Wikström's eight-message strengthening. Parallel repetition is only unconditionally safe for arguments of at most three rounds.
Håstad, Pass, Wikström, and Pietrzak: parallel repetition does decay exponentially for public-coin arguments, which is the case every deployed system is in. This is one of the concrete reasons public-coin matters.
Query repetition in FRI is a different operation from repeating the protocol — same exponent, different object. Which one a parameter table means.
How repetition interacts with the round-by-round error, with grinding, and with proof size; and whether fixed-weight repetition variants change the accounting.

Sources: Bellare, Impagliazzo, and Naor, Does Parallel Repetition Lower the Error in Computationally Sound Protocols? (FOCS 1997); Pietrzak and Wikström, Parallel Repetition of Computationally Sound Protocols Revisited; Håstad, Pass, Wikström, and Pietrzak on public-coin arguments.

Knowledge soundness says a prover who convinces the verifier knows a witness. It does not say a prover who has seen valid proofs cannot produce a new one without knowing anything, and that is the property an on-chain verifier needs, since every proof it has ever accepted is public.

Questions this page should answer:
Simulation extractability, weak and strong, and how each differs from knowledge soundness — the extractor now works against an adversary with access to simulated proofs.
Groth16's malleability, the concrete attacks it has enabled, and why proof uniqueness is a separate property from soundness.
Whether Fiat–Shamir in the random oracle model gives simulation extractability for free, and for which classes of protocol.
What a contract actually needs: replay protection by binding the proof to the statement, or the cryptographic property. Where nullifiers and domain separation substitute for it.
Whether anything in ArkLib states it, and what a Lean statement would have to quantify over.

Sources: How to Prove False Statements for why the distinctions are not academic; On Soundness Notions for Interactive Oracle Proofs for the implications between them; ArkLib's OracleReduction/Security for the same map in Lean.

The step from an interactive public-coin protocol to a proof that can be sent as a string. When the protocol is an IOP, the BCS transform realises the oracles and Fiat–Shamir removes the interaction; when it is already an IP, Fiat–Shamir is the whole compilation. A soundness theorem about the interactive protocol does not automatically apply to the result.

The pipeline: which steps, in which order, and what each assumes about the protocol.
What the compiled adversary can do that the interactive one cannot — grinding, restoring prefixes — and which soundness notions constrain it.

The compilation loss: how the interactive error becomes a non-interactive one, and when the bound is vacuous.

ArkLib's organising abstraction, and the reason it can hope to cover many protocols rather than one. A reduction maps one relation to another; a protocol is a composition of reductions; completeness and soundness are proved once per component.

The mathematics the protocols are built out of. Most of the recent performance work lives here rather than in the protocol layer: the same FRI-shaped argument became an order of magnitude faster because the field changed, not because the argument did.
This is also the part of the stack CompPoly is about — fields, polynomials, and their computable representations — so these pages should stay close to what is actually definable in Lean.

fr:title.text: Cyclic Groups and the Discrete Logarithm

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Cyclic Groups and the Discrete Logarithm

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The setting the classical proofs of knowledge are stated over. A cyclic group G of prime order q with generator g: every element of G is g^w for exactly one exponent w in \mathbb {Z}_q, so exponentiation is a bijection from \mathbb {Z}_q to G and exponent arithmetic is arithmetic in a prime field. The discrete logarithm problem is to invert that bijection — given h \in G, find w with g^w = h — and it is assumed hard in the groups used in practice, which are elliptic curve groups over a large prime field.

Questions this page should answer:
Cyclic group, order, generator; why prime order rather than merely cyclic, and what breaks at composite order.
Why prime q makes every nonzero exponent difference invertible — the single step Schnorr extraction turns on.
The discrete logarithm assumption and its relatives, computational and decisional Diffie–Hellman, and which of them a given sigma protocol actually needs.
What is known about the hardness: generic-group lower bounds, index calculus, and why elliptic curves rather than the multiplicative group of a prime field.
Where the setting reappears later in the corpus: the inner-product arguments that scale it to logarithmic proofs, and the pairing-based line that asks more of the curve than a group law.
Why this setting is absent from the FRI family, and what replaces the group structure there — fields and codes.
Post-quantum status: Shor breaks all of it, which is the reason the lattice protocols exist.
Reading: Boneh and Shoup, A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography, for the assumptions and their relations; Thaler, Proofs, Arguments, and Zero-Knowledge, for how they enter the proof systems.

fr:title.text: Finite Fields and the Small-Field Turn

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Finite Fields and the Small-Field Turn

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Transparent provers migrated from 256-bit scalar fields down to 31-bit primes and then to \mathbb {F}_2. The migration is the single largest source of speedup in the last five years, and it constrains everything above it.

Questions this page should answer:
Prime fields, extension fields, and why the prover wants a small base field while soundness wants a large challenge space.
The specific fields and what makes each fast: Mersenne31 (2^{31}-1), BabyBear, KoalaBear, Goldilocks.
Where extension-field arithmetic is unavoidable — challenges, DEEP queries, batching — and how much of the trace can stay in the base field.
Packing and vectorisation: how field choice interacts with the machine.
What is lost: two-adicity, FFT-friendliness, and the circle workaround.
Sources: The Small-Field Turn in Succinct Proofs.

The tower \mathbb {F}_2 \subset \mathbb {F}_{2^2} \subset \mathbb {F}_{2^4} \subset \cdots \subset \mathbb {F}_{2^{128}}, built by iterated quadratic extension, and the arithmetic that makes it attractive. This is the ground Binius stands on.

Questions this page should answer:
The tower construction, and why every subfield embedding is free.
Why binary: no modular reduction, characteristic 2 arithmetic maps onto bit operations, and small values cost small fields.
The claimed cost comparison against Mersenne31, and under what measure it holds.
Multilinear polynomials over a tower, and why the multilinear setting rather than the univariate one.
Ring switching: moving between tower levels inside a single argument.
Sources: Binary tower fields (Irreducible), SNARKs on binary fields (LambdaClass), The Small-Field Turn.

Two representations of the same data, supporting different arguments. The univariate world pairs with low-degree testing; the multilinear world pairs with sumcheck. Knowing which one a protocol lives in explains most of its shape.

Questions this page should answer:
The multilinear extension of a function on the Boolean hypercube; uniqueness; the equality polynomial and its role.
Degree versus number of variables as the size parameter, and what each buys.
Why FRI wants univariate and Basefold, HyperPlonk, and Binius want multilinear.
How WHIR unifies the two, and what the translation costs.
Computable representations — dense, sparse, coefficient, evaluation form — and which operations each makes cheap. This is CompPoly's design problem.

fr:title.text: Evaluation Domains, FFTs, and Circle Groups

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Evaluation Domains, FFTs, and Circle Groups

Named systems, each a particular choice of arithmetisation, commitment, and field. Once the layers below are understood these should be readable as combinations rather than as separate inventions — and where a system is not just a combination, that is the interesting part.
Three group elements, a circuit-specific trusted setup, and a verifier cheap enough for the EVM. Obsolete as a zkVM backend and unavoidable as a wrapper.

QAPs: from R1CS to a divisibility claim.
The proof and the verification equation; why it is exactly three elements.

Circuit-specific setup as the practical objection, and what universal setup changed.
The system that made Plonkish a category, and the implementation that most auditors' intuitions were formed on.

The protocol: gate identity, permutation argument, quotient, and opening.

R1CS proved with sumcheck instead of quotients, which removes the FFT and moves the cost into a sparse polynomial commitment. It is also one of the systems ArkLib has formalised, so it is a good place to read a full argument in Lean.

The reduction from R1CS satisfiability to a sumcheck claim.
Sparse polynomial commitment (Spark) and why the matrices' sparsity is what makes this cheap.
Prover cost profile against a Plonkish system on the same circuit.
The line from here to HyperNova, which folds the same shape of claim.

Plonkish constraints over the Boolean hypercube rather than a multiplicative subgroup, so the prover never runs an FFT. The clearest statement of what moving to multilinear representations does and does not buy.

Questions this page should answer:
The translation of gate and wiring constraints into sumcheck claims.
What replaces the quotient polynomial and the low-degree test.
Cost profile: no FFT, more commitment work, different memory behaviour.
High-degree custom gates, which this handles better than univariate Plonk.

fr:title.text: STARKs: Plonky3, Stwo, and Circle STARKs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: STARKs: Plonky3, Stwo, and Circle STARKs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AIR plus FRI, over a small field, as a reusable toolkit rather than a single protocol. This is the layer the Rust-to-Lean extraction work targets: Plonky3 in Lean, with proofs about what it computes.

Questions this page should answer:
The STARK protocol end to end: trace, constraints, quotient, commitment, low-degree test.
Plonky3 as a toolkit — what is configurable (field, hash, PCS, folding factor) and what is fixed.
Stwo and the circle domain: Mersenne31 has no large smooth subgroup, so what replaces it and what changes in the constraint system.
Circle STARKs' vanishing polynomials and the extra care their boundary constraints need.
Where the two toolkits agree, since both consume an AIR — and what that means for Clean targeting both.
Sources: Plonky3, stwo, Buterin, Exploring circle STARKs.

A proof system built from the ground up on binary tower fields, with ring switching as the mechanism that keeps small values cheap. The most complete demonstration of the small-field argument taken to its limit.

Questions this page should answer:
The stack: tower fields, multilinear polynomials, a small-field commitment, and sumcheck-based constraint checking.
How a bit-level computation avoids paying for embedding into a large field.
Flock, which specialises the same idea to large batches of one Boolean circuit and is what made conventional hashes cheap enough to prove that Ethereum dropped Poseidon.
Where the extension field is still required, and what fraction of the work it accounts for.
The measured comparison against 31-bit prime systems, and on which workloads it holds.
ArkLib's ProofSystem/Binius and RingSwitching: what is stated and what is proved.
Sources: Binary tower fields, SNARKs on binary fields, ArkLib.

How a proof about a long computation is assembled from proofs about short ones. Every zkVM that proves a real workload is doing this, and it is where the soundness argument becomes hardest to keep track of — the Nova bug is the standing example.
The definitions that folding and recursion are trying to achieve, and the overhead problem that shapes every construction: the verifier has to be expressible as a circuit in the system it verifies.

Questions this page should answer:
Incrementally verifiable computation and proof-carrying data: the statements, and the knowledge soundness they require.
Recursion overhead: what a verifier-in-circuit costs, and which components dominate (hashing, MSM, field arithmetic).
Cycles of curves, and why hash-based systems avoid the problem differently.
How the security loss compounds over recursion depth.

Folding two R1CS instances into one without proving either, deferring all the SNARK work to the end. Also a case study in why this material needs formalising: a soundness bug was found in the published scheme.

Questions this page should answer:
Relaxed R1CS and committed relaxed R1CS: why the relaxation is needed to make folding close.
The folding step and its knowledge-soundness argument.
Why the recursive circuit is small — the folding verifier, not a SNARK verifier.
The bug: what the flaw was, what it permitted, and which part of the argument would have caught it under machine-checked scrutiny.
Sources: how Nova got broken, awesome-folding.
The folding design space after Nova: which constraint systems can be folded, how many instances at once, and what the recursive circuit costs.

Questions this page should answer:
HyperNova: folding CCS, with per-step cost dominated by one MSM.
ProtoStar: folding arbitrary low-degree polynomial maps, and what that generality buys.
ProtoGalaxy and multi-instance folding; KiloNova and non-uniform PCD.
The axes to compare on: constraint system, instances per fold, recursive circuit size, assumptions.
Which of these is the right target for a formalisation, given that the definitions are still moving.
Sources: HyperNova, multi-instance folding techniques, awesome-folding.
Splitting a long execution into segments that can be proved independently and in parallel. The mechanism that makes zkVM proving a distributed job rather than a single machine's problem.

Questions this page should answer:
Segmenting a trace: what state must be carried across a boundary, and how it is committed.
The consistency argument between shards, especially for memory.
Aggregating shard proofs into one, and the recursion tree's shape.
How SP1 and RISC Zero each do it, and what their differences imply.
The soundness surface this adds — a shard boundary is a place to forget a constraint.
The last step of a deployed pipeline: convert a large STARK proof into something an on-chain verifier can check cheaply, usually by proving the STARK verifier inside a pairing-based system.

Questions this page should answer:
The wrapping chain in a real system, layer by layer, with proof sizes at each step.
Arithmetising a hash-based verifier: which parts are expensive and why.
Gas cost of the final verifier, and what it constrains upstream.
The trust and assumption stack the wrap introduces — a trusted setup at the end of a transparent pipeline.
Whether the composed security is stated anywhere precisely enough to formalise.

Everything above, wrapped around an instruction set so that a program rather than a circuit is the thing being proved. A zkVM decomposes into three layers — the ISA, the VM architecture, and the proving layer — and most design disagreements are about where to put work between them.

This is the object the verified zkEVM effort is ultimately aimed at. A machine semantics in Lean is the first half of the statement one wants to prove about a zkVM; LC3 in Lean is that half at small scale.
A map of the layers, so that a claim about one system can be compared with a claim about another. Worth writing before the pages below it.

Questions this page should answer:
The three layers — ISA, VM architecture, proving layer — and the interface between each pair.
What "proving a program" means formally: the relation being proved, and where the program commitment enters.
Which layer a given optimisation belongs to, and which choices are genuinely independent.
The end-to-end statement a zkVM claims, written out in full.
Sources: SoK: Understanding zkVM, Projects that shaped modern zkVMs.

Whether to prove an existing ISA or design one for provability. RISC-V won the general-purpose end by bringing a compiler toolchain with it; the custom VMs argue the constraint cost is worth the loss.

Questions this page should answer:
RISC-V (RV32I and extensions) as a target: what makes each instruction class expensive to constrain.
Register machines versus stack machines (Miden, zkWasm), and what the memory argument looks like in each.
Purpose-built ISAs — Cairo, Valida — and the specific constraint-cost arguments for them.
Instruction decomposition and the lookup-based approach to semantics that Jolt takes.
The formal ISA specification: what the Sail-to-Lean route gives, and what it does not.
How an execution becomes a set of tables. In practice this is where a zkVM's engineering lives, and the details are what Clean has to be able to express.

Questions this page should answer:
Chips as separate AIRs, one per operation class, connected by cross-table lookups.
The main trace against auxiliary and preprocessed columns; what each costs to commit.
Padding to a power of two, and the constraints that must hold on padded rows.
Witness generation as a first-class cost, and whether the generator is verified against the constraints.
How a single instruction's semantics is spread across chips, and how the pieces are tied back together.

Random-access memory is the hardest part of a zkVM to constrain and the most common source of unsoundness. The general machinery is in permutation and memory arguments; this page is about what the systems actually do.

Questions this page should answer:
Read-write RAM by offline memory checking, as in SP1, Jolt, and RISC Zero.
Paged memory with Merkle verification, which RISC Zero also supports, and when that is preferable.
Stack-based models (Miden, zkWasm) and how their consistency arguments differ.
Memory across shard boundaries — the argument that ties independent segments together.
The concrete cost of a load or store, counted in trace cells and lookups.
Sources: SoK: Understanding zkVM, Nebula.

Hand-written circuits for hot operations — hashes, elliptic-curve arithmetic, big-integer work — invoked from the VM instead of being proved instruction by instruction. Large speedups, and a large increase in the amount of hand-written constrained code that has to be correct.

Questions this page should answer:
The mechanism: how a precompile attaches to the trace and how its inputs and outputs are tied to VM state.
The speedups claimed, and on which workloads they decide the benchmark.
The soundness surface: an under-constrained precompile is a complete break, with no compiler to catch it.
Extensibility as a design goal, and what a user-supplied precompile has to prove.
Why this is the most valuable place in the stack to point Clean at.
One entry per system: backend, arithmetisation, field, memory model, and the choice that distinguishes it. The point is a comparison table, not a survey.

Questions this page should answer:
SP1 — RISC-V on Plonky3, precompile-heavy.
Jolt — Lasso-based, lookups for instruction semantics, notably small proofs.
RISC Zero — RISC-V, read-write and paged Merkle memory.
OpenVM — modular and extensible by construction; what its extension interface requires.
Stwo and Cairo — circle STARKs over Mersenne31, with a purpose-built ISA.
Miden and Valida — stack machine and provability-first ISA respectively.
For each: what its soundness rests on that the others' does not.

What actually costs time, and how to read a published comparison. The target is a cost model good enough to predict the direction of a change before measuring it.

The cost breakdown: witness generation, hashing, FFTs, MSMs, extension-field arithmetic.
Cycles per second as a metric, and what it hides — precompiles, shard size, security parameters.
Proof size and verifier time across systems, and the recursion that produces the final numbers.
How the field choice shows up in measurements, and why hash rate is often the real headline.
Comparing at equal security: the benchmark question that is usually skipped.

A catalogue of real failure modes, kept concrete. This page is the evidence for the formalisation work, so it should stay evidence rather than argument. Smart contract vulnerabilities due to poor specification is the same catalogue one domain over, and the failure modes rhyme: code that did what it was specified to do, and a specification that permitted what nobody intended.

Questions this page should answer:
Under-constrained circuits: the general shape, and the canonical examples.
Missing range checks, and why a forgotten monotonicity constraint on memory timestamps is fatal.
Fiat–Shamir misuse: transcripts missing a value, weak domain separation, insufficient challenge space.
Soundness bugs in published schemes rather than implementations — Nova is the example to write up.
Parameter errors: a security level computed in the wrong regime.
Which of these a type system, a linter, an audit, or a proof would each have caught.
Sources: how Nova got broken, How to Prove False Statements.

The reason the rest of this corpus is organised the way it is. The verified zkEVM effort runs three tracks — the zkVM constraints, the EVM semantics, and the cryptography — and ArkLib and CompPoly are the cryptography track.

These pages stay closer to the code than the rest of the corpus, which also makes them the ones most likely to go stale. Related: protocol snarkification, computable specifications, formal verification in proof assistants.
A modular library of formally verified arguments of knowledge in Lean, organised around interactive oracle reductions rather than around individual protocols.

Questions this page should answer:
The directory structure as a design argument: OracleReduction, Commitments, ProofSystem, AGM, and the To* compatibility layers.
What is formalised and to what depth — sumcheck, Spartan, FRI, STIR, WHIR, Binius, Merkle trees, coding theory.
ProofSystem/ConstraintSystem: R1CS, Plonk, lookup, and memory checking in one place.
The security definitions in OracleReduction/Security, which are the real contribution.
What is a statement with no proof yet, and what the roadmap prioritises.
Which developments are blocked on CompPoly.
Sources: ArkLib, ArkLib on lean-lang.org.

Computable polynomials and finite fields in Lean: an executable mirror of the Mathlib definitions, with transfer theorems so proofs can be done on the noncomputable side. The case for computable specifications is made elsewhere; this page is about the artefact.

Questions this page should answer:
The representations chosen, and which operations each makes cheap. See univariate and multilinear polynomials.
The transfer pattern: computable definition, Mathlib definition, proven equivalence, and how proofs move across it.
Field representations and the small fields that matter — see the small-field turn.

hax and its Lean backend: what Rust it accepts, and what it does with the parts it does not.

fr:title.text: Specifying the Machine: Sail, LLZK, zkLean

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Specifying the Machine: Sail, LLZK, zkLean

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The other half of a verified zkVM: a trustworthy specification of the machine being proved, and a way to reason about circuits written in the many DSLs that exist. LC3 in Lean is the same problem at a scale small enough to see all of it.

The Sail Lean backend: extracting the RISC-V specification into Lean, and what fidelity that gives.
LLZK as an MLIR dialect unifying circuits from different DSLs — what it can and cannot express.
zkLean for R1CS, alongside Clean for AIR.

fr:title.text: What a Verified zkVM Would Mean

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What a Verified zkVM Would Mean

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The statement at the top of the whole effort, written out honestly: which theorems compose, and which links in the chain are assumptions rather than proofs. It is the claim the whole effort will be judged on, and its general form is the issue of incorrect specification: a machine-checked proof is only ever as good as the statement it proves.

Questions this page should answer:
The chain: ISA specification, constraint system, arithmetisation soundness, IOP soundness, commitment security, Fiat–Shamir, recursion, extracted implementation.
Which links are proved today, which are stated, and which are not formalised at all.
The irreducible assumptions: hash security, conjectured proximity bounds, the compiler, the hardware.
Whether "verified" should mean the composed end-to-end theorem, or a set of component theorems with audited seams.
The 2027 target the project set, and what would have to be true for it to be met.
Sources: verified-zkevm.org, Verified-zkEVM overview.

The constraints that come from the deployment target rather than the mathematics. Ethereum wants blocks proved in seconds, on modest hardware, at a security level nobody is willing to negotiate — and increasingly with post-quantum assumptions. See protocol snarkification for the broader effort, and Safely Snarkifying the Ethereum Protocol for the talk.

fr:title.text: Real-Time Proving and the zkEVM Target

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Real-Time Proving and the zkEVM Target

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What the protocol actually asks of a prover, stated as numbers, and which part of the stack each number constrains.

Questions this page should answer:
The current latency, cost, hardware, and proof-size targets, with a source for each.
Proving an L1 block: what dominates — hashing, signature verification, state access.
Verification on the consumer side: what a home verifier must be able to check, and in what time.
Multi-prover and diversity arguments, and what they assume about implementation independence.
Which targets are met today and which are not.
The hash function is usually the prover's largest single cost, so primitive choice is a proof-system decision rather than an implementation detail.

That framing is what the August 2026 decision to drop Poseidon for L1 inverts, and this page should be written with the reversal in view: hash-friendly SNARKs rather than SNARK-friendly hashes. The cost question below is still the right question — the answer simply stopped selecting for an exotic primitive.

Questions this page should answer:
Arithmetisation-friendly hashes (Poseidon2 and relatives) against standard ones (Keccak, SHA-256, Blake3), counted in constraints.
The security tradeoff: young algebraic designs against well-analysed bit-oriented ones.
Where Ethereum has no choice — Keccak in the state trie, ECDSA in transactions — and what those cost.
Hash rate as a headline benchmark, and what it does and does not predict.
Which hash a Merkle commitment should use at each layer of a recursion.
Hash-based proof systems are plausibly post-quantum and pairing-based ones are not, which turns a cryptographic deadline into an architectural constraint on wrapping.

Questions this page should answer:
What is at risk and what is not: discrete-log commitments, hash-based commitments, the ROM analysis in a quantum setting.
Hash-based signatures and aggregation, and why a SNARK is the aggregation mechanism. Which hash they are instantiated with is now SHA-2 or BLAKE rather than Poseidon.
Lattice-based commitments as an alternative, and their cost profile.
The consequence for the last step of a pipeline that currently ends in Groth16.
What VCV-io's lattice work already covers.
What bit-security a deployed system actually claims, under which assumptions, and who checked. This is where soundness regimes stop being a theoretical distinction.

Questions this page should answer:
The parameters real provers ship: rate, repetitions, grinding bits, field size — and the claimed level they add up to.
Which claims depend on a conjecture, and whether that is documented in the system's own materials.
The accounting across recursion layers, where errors compose.
Who is responsible for the number: protocol designers, implementers, or auditors.
What a machine-checked parameter calculation would look like, and whether it is a reasonable thing to build.

An order to read in, so that filling the corpus out does not turn into breadth-first browsing. Systematisations first, because they fix the vocabulary and the attributions; then the primary sources; then the code.

In order:

SoK: Hash-Based Polynomial Commitments and Low-Degree Tests — the whole FRI-to-WHIR lineage in one place, with the soundness regimes kept straight.
The Small-Field Turn in Succinct Proofs — field choice as the organising story of recent performance work.
SoK: Understanding zkVM — the layer decomposition and a comparison across real systems.
Primary sources, in lineage order: FRI, DEEP-FRI, STIR, WHIR; then Basefold and Binius.
How to Prove False Statements — read after the soundness notions, not before.
ArkLib, starting from OracleReduction/Basic.lean and the sumcheck development.
clean and a Plonky3 AIR side by side — the same circuit in both.
A page in this corpus is done when its main theorem can be stated with its assumptions, and what breaks when one of them is dropped. Everything else is note-taking.

There are ongoing efforts to "snarkify" Ethereum, i.e. to integrate zero knowledge proofs into every layer of the Ethereum protocol. I contribute to this via formal verification in Lean. My main focus is currently on CompPoly and Arklib.
See our website for more information.
A systematic study of the underlying cryptography, topic by topic, is collected in zkVMs and SNARKs.

We have spent the last few months travelling. I'm writing this in May 2026 from Rome. The most recent two trips were Cannes (for EthCC) and Paris (for SViL26). SViL26 was one of the most productive trips yet, only rivaled by HACS. We are now at a point where we can feasibly extract Plonky3 from Rust into Lean and formally prove things!

In my talk today at zkproofs8, I showed a minimal example of formally verifying Koalabear in Plonky3, in Lean. We're making fast progress on CompPoly, Arklib, and now with the tooling where it's at it looks like it's time to start to marry them and actually formally verifying real code in Lean!

Once I'm back from Rome, I will basically be full-time on this problem. This is good for me because I have so far avoided learning too much about cryptography, and now that I'll be staring at the implementations in Rust as well as the formal specs, it will be hard to avoid actually understanding things. I'm hoping that this process will stimulate Arklib into grater maturity, starting with CompPoly; I'm also hoping that the tooling will get a lot better (with my help) through this project. This will be the main thing this summer, hoping that by the end of the summer we have serious formal proofs of Plonky3!

We attended HACS and RWC26 in Taipei in early March, which was extremely productive. I learned a lot about Hax and Aeneas, verified compilers, and cryptography in general. Got strong insights for the upcoming work, and had a chance to evangelize our work on CompPoly. Bolton Bailey and I had a great conversation about the (many many) applications of computable polynomials in Lean. I hope that we can upstream CompPoly to CSLib and have many people using and maintaining it.
